blocks.text: …if it is to stay relaxed
The “sit” procedure is suitable for situations in which our dog is exposed to little or unproblematic distraction and we want to build a framework of order.
“Sit” lends itself to all everyday and frequently recurring situations – likewise to play situations and to moments in which we want to put the dog into an attentive and motivated basic mood.

“Sit” can serve as a provisional alternative in difficult situations if the dog does not yet master the “down” reliably. In this case, however, the stability is clearly lower than with the “down”. “Sit” should therefore only be used as a bridging exercise and be replaced by “down” as soon as possible.
Start, prerequisites & training frequency 📅
Start: From about the 12th week of age.
Training frequency: Daily, in all situations that present themselves.
Progression: Starting without distraction and, over time, under growing stimulus levels.
Execution & training environment 🐕
Ideally we train “sit” during the walk while on the leash: address the dog by name to establish attention, then stop and calmly say “sit”.

The flat hand gently supports on the croup (the rear area above the hind legs), while the leash helps the dog to hold the position. The entire procedure may and should be accompanied calmly and attentively with the word “sit”.
Remember: Our voice is the bridge to the dog.
Step 1: Establish attention & give the cue 👁️
Address the dog by name, stop and calmly give the cue “sit”. The leash supports by holding the position, and the flat hand on the croup gently guides the dog into the sit.
Step 2: Build a calm pause & patient staying in the sit ⏳
As soon as the dog sits, we stay calm and pause. As training success progresses, this pause can be extended in time – this is how we build patient staying in the sit.
If the dog gets up in between, we patiently and without pressure correct it back into the sit.
Step 3: Eye contact & praise 🌟
Address the dog very calmly by name so that it looks at us. This “looking at us” is fundamental to training success.
If the dog sits calmly and looks at us, we praise it affectionately and stroke its head soothingly.
Remember: Calm voice and praise are the consequence of the dog looking at us – of its mentally “being with us” in the sit. This is essential for future learning success.
Step 4: Progress – sit in front of the handler 🔄
As success progresses, we increasingly shape the “sit” – as already applied in the section “Leash work” – so that the dog regularly sits in front of us, facing us.

After the cue “sit”, we walk a few steps backwards and thereby get the dog to turn around, come towards us in a praising tone of voice and find its way to sit in front of us. This variant will later be a great help to us in situations rich in distraction.
What you should avoid ⚠️
Avoid sharply spoken commands in training and in everyday use.
Avoid permanently keeping the leash short during the sit.
Avoid sitting turned away from the handler.
Avoid praise for inattentive sitting.
Avoid stress during the sit procedure.
Practical impulse: The daily sit moment

Use everyday situations – waiting at the kerb, greeting acquaintances, the pause on a walk – as natural training moments for calm, attentive sitting. These short, relaxed repetitions in real life are more valuable than any isolated training session.
→ Did I make sure of a stress-free environment at the beginning?
→ Did I speak to my dog calmly?
→ Was my dog calm during the exercise?
→ Did I correct calmly but purposefully?
→ Did I make sure the dog sat securely and calmly before I praised?
→ Did I observe calm communication with the dog?
→ Did I walk backwards enough for support?
→ Was the leash always loose while walking and in the sit?
→ Did the dog seek eye contact with me?
→ Did I praise calmly and intensively?
